title: Pluto's bullies
q: Natural satellites in the Solar System that are bigger than Pluto
rule: Pluto is about 2,377 km across. Our own satellite counts.
fact: Triton orbits Neptune backwards, strong evidence that it was captured from the Kuiper Belt, the same region Pluto comes from.

traps.Titania: Uranus's biggest moon is only about 1,580 km across.
traps.Charon: Pluto's own moon is about half Pluto's width.
traps.Enceladus: Famous for its geysers, but only about 500 km across.
traps.Rhea: Saturn's second-largest moon is about 1,530 km across, still smaller than Pluto.
traps.Iapetus: Saturn's two-tone moon is about 1,470 km across.

title: Leaving home
q: Crewed Apollo missions that left Earth orbit
rule: A flight that looped around the Moon without landing counts. Apollo 1 never flew and Apollo 4 to 6 had no crew.
fact: Apollo 10's lunar module, Snoopy, skimmed to about 15 km above the Moon in a full dress rehearsal for the landing, without touching down.

traps.Apollo 7: The first crewed Apollo flight stayed in Earth orbit.
traps.Apollo 9: It tested the lunar module, but only in Earth orbit.
traps.Apollo 1: It never flew: the crew died in a launch-pad fire in 1967.
traps.Apollo-Soyuz: The 1975 handshake in space happened in Earth orbit.

title: Fly by night
q: Constellations named after a real bird
rule: Official IAU constellations only. Mythical birds such as the phoenix do not count.
fact: Apus, the bird of paradise, means 'no feet' in Greek: early specimens reached Europe with their feet removed, so people thought the birds never landed.

traps.Phoenix: It is a real constellation, but the phoenix is a mythical bird.
traps.Pegasus: A winged horse, not a bird.
traps.Draco: The dragon is mythical, and not a bird anyway.
traps.Lyra: It depicts a lyre, a musical instrument.

title: Right stuff
q: Members of NASA's original Mercury Seven
rule: The seven astronauts NASA announced in April 1959, whether or not they ever flew a Mercury mission.
fact: Deke Slayton was grounded for a heart condition and finally reached space in 1975, aged 51, on the Apollo-Soyuz mission.

traps.Neil Armstrong: He joined NASA in 1962, in the second astronaut group.
traps.Buzz Aldrin: He was picked in 1963, in the third astronaut group.
traps.Yuri Gagarin: A Soviet cosmonaut, not a NASA astronaut.
traps.Chuck Yeager: The famous test pilot had no college degree, so he was never eligible.
traps.Jim Lovell: He was picked in 1962, in the second astronaut group.

title: Unit of honour
q: SI units named after a real person
rule: Base units and named derived units only. Non-SI units such as the gauss or the curie do not count.
fact: The gray and the sievert are both one joule per kilogram; the sievert just adds a weighting for how harmful the radiation is to living tissue.

traps.Fahrenheit: A person's name, but not an SI unit: the kelvin and the Celsius degree are the SI temperature units.
traps.Gauss: A CGS unit named after a person; the SI unit of magnetic flux density is the tesla.
traps.Curie: An older radioactivity unit, replaced in SI by the becquerel.
traps.Decibel: It honours Alexander Graham Bell, but it is not an SI unit.
traps.Mole: It comes from 'molecule', not from a person called Avogadro.

title: Deep time
q: Geological periods of the Phanerozoic, the last 539 million years
rule: The 12 periods of the current eon. Epochs (Eocene, Pleistocene), eras (Mesozoic) and the proposed Anthropocene do not count.
fact: Tyrannosaurus rex lived closer in time to us than to Stegosaurus: Stegosaurus was Jurassic, and T. rex came some 80 million years later.

traps.Pleistocene: The Ice Age epoch is part of the Quaternary period, not a period itself.
traps.Holocene: Our own epoch is part of the Quaternary period.
traps.Mesozoic: An era, made up of the Triassic, Jurassic and Cretaceous periods.
traps.Anthropocene: Proposed, but geological authorities rejected it as an official unit in 2024.
traps.Ediacaran: A real period, but it ended just before the Cambrian began.

title: Lend a hand
q: Bones in the human hand and wrist
rule: Individual bones count, and so do the general names for each group. Forearm and foot bones do not.
fact: The pea-shaped pisiform is the smallest wrist bone, and it is really a sesamoid: a bone that grows inside a tendon, like the kneecap.

traps.Radius: A forearm bone: it meets the wrist but is not part of it.
traps.Ulna: A forearm bone, not a hand or wrist bone.
traps.Metatarsal: That is the foot's version of the metacarpal.
traps.Talus: The ankle bone, in the foot.
traps.Cuboid: A bone of the foot, not the hand.

title: Nerve centre
q: The twelve cranial nerves
rule: Give each nerve's name, with or without the word 'nerve'. Nerves that leave the spinal cord, like the sciatic, do not count.
fact: The trochlear nerve is the only cranial nerve to leave the brainstem from the back, and it drives a single muscle, the superior oblique of the eye.

traps.Sciatic nerve: It runs from the lower spine down the leg, so it is a spinal nerve.
traps.Ulnar nerve: The 'funny bone' nerve is a spinal nerve running down the arm.
traps.Median nerve: A spinal nerve of the arm and hand.
traps.Phrenic nerve: It serves the diaphragm and arises from the neck's spinal nerves.
traps.Radial nerve: A spinal nerve of the arm.

title: Monkey business
q: Types of ape alive today
rule: Monkeys and lemurs do not count, and extinct apes are out.
fact: Gibraltar's famous 'Barbary apes' are tailless macaques, so they are monkeys, and the only wild monkeys in Europe.

traps.Baboon: A baboon is an Old World monkey with a tail.
traps.Barbary ape: Despite the name, the Gibraltar 'apes' are tailless macaques, which are monkeys.
traps.Mandrill: The colourful-faced mandrill is a monkey.
traps.Spider monkey: A New World monkey with a long grasping tail.
traps.Lemur: Lemurs are more distant primates, neither monkeys nor apes.

title: Going large
q: Metric prefixes that mean a million or more
rule: Official SI prefixes only. Binary prefixes like mebi and informal words like googol do not count.
fact: Ronna and quetta, adopted in 2022, were the first new SI prefixes since 1991, when yotta, zetta, yocto and zepto arrived.

traps.Kilo: Only a thousand, which is smaller than a million.
traps.Mebi: A binary prefix (2 to the power 20), not an SI prefix.
traps.Googol: A huge number, but not a metric prefix.

title: Wild at heart
q: Wild cat species native to the Americas
rule: Living species only. Domestic and feral cats, extinct cats like Smilodon, and colour forms like the 'black panther' do not count.
fact: The margay can rotate its hind ankles 180 degrees, so it can climb down trees headfirst like a squirrel.

traps.Leopard: Leopards live in Africa and Asia. The big spotted cat of the Americas is the jaguar.
traps.Lion: Wild lions live in Africa and India. America's lions died out about 11,000 years ago.
traps.Cheetah: Cheetahs live in Africa, with a tiny group in Iran. None live in the Americas.
traps.Black panther: Not a species: it is a dark leopard or jaguar.
traps.Iberian lynx: That one lives in Spain and Portugal.

title: Oh deer
q: Deer species living free in the British countryside
rule: Herds living free count, including one introduced herd in the Scottish Highlands. Deer kept only in parks or zoos do not count.
fact: Chinese water deer have no antlers but grow long tusk-like canine teeth, and escapes from Woburn gave Britain a big share of the world's wild population.

traps.Elk: Elk (what Americans call moose) died out in Britain thousands of years ago.
traps.Pere David's deer: Only kept in parks, such as Woburn, not living free.
traps.Stag: A stag is a male deer, not a species.
traps.Hind: A hind is a female red deer, not a species.

title: Tit for tat
q: British birds with 'tit' in their name that breed in Britain
rule: The species must breed regularly in Britain and have 'tit' in its common name, even if it isn't a true tit.
fact: The bearded tit isn't a tit at all: it's a reedling that lives in reed beds, and its 'beard' is a black moustache on the male.

title: Many sides
q: Polygon shapes with between 3 and 12 sides, by their standard names
rule: Only the standard names for a polygon with that many sides count; shape types like rhombus don't.
fact: Every polygon's interior angles add up to (n minus 2) times 180 degrees, so a dodecagon's angles total 1,800 degrees.

traps.Rhombus: A rhombus is one specific four-sided shape, not the general name for a four-sided polygon.

title: Month's stone
q: Gemstones on the modern list of birthstones
rule: Any stone on the modern Jewelers of America list, for any month.
fact: Spinel became August's third birthstone in 2016, the first change to the American list since tanzanite joined December in 2002.

traps.Jade: A traditional gift for some anniversaries, but not on the modern birthstone list.
traps.Onyx: On some older lists, not the modern one.
traps.Amber: A fossil resin, not on the list.

title: Type cast
q: The eight common ABO and Rh blood types
rule: Combine each of the four main blood groups with either Rh sign; there is no group C.
fact: People with O negative blood are called universal red cell donors, while AB positive people are universal recipients.

traps.Type C: There's no C group: the ABO system has only A, B, AB and O.

title: Down the hatch
q: Digestive tract organs, from the top of the throat to the bowel's end
rule: Only hollow organs in the food tube count; the liver, pancreas and gallbladder are accessory organs and don't.
fact: The small intestine is roughly 6 to 7 metres long in an adult, while the large intestine is only about 1.5 metres, despite its name.

traps.Liver: It's an accessory digestive organ, not part of the food tube itself.
traps.Anus: It's the opening at the end of the canal, not an organ.

title: Force of nature
q: The names of the Beaufort wind forces, 0 to 12
rule: Met Office names, with the usual international alternatives accepted. Give each force's full name rather than a fragment.
fact: The Beaufort scale was devised in 1805 by Royal Navy officer Francis Beaufort, who judged wind strength by its effects on sails at sea.

traps.Tornado: Tornadoes aren't on the Beaufort scale, which stops at force 12.
traps.Breeze: Too vague: each force has its own full name, such as 'Fresh breeze'.

title: Four rooms
q: The four chambers and four valves of the human heart
rule: Only the named chambers and valves count; the septum, the walls between chambers, and blood vessels don't.
fact: The mitral valve gets its name from its resemblance to a bishop's mitre, the tall pointed hat.

traps.Septum: It's the wall between the chambers, not a chamber or a valve.
traps.Aorta: It's a blood vessel leaving the heart, not a valve or chamber.

title: Blood brothers
q: Blood cell types, including the five white cell types
rule: Only the specific named types count, not the umbrella term 'white blood cell'.
fact: Basophils are the rarest white blood cells, usually making up less than 1 percent of them, yet they release histamine during allergic reactions.

traps.White blood cell: That's the umbrella term for the group, not one of the named types.
traps.Neuron: It's a nerve cell, not a type of blood cell.

title: Saturn's set
q: Moons of Saturn with a diameter over 200 km
rule: Mean diameter must be above 200 km; smaller Saturn moons such as Janus don't count.
fact: Titan is bigger than the planet Mercury and is the only moon known to have a thick atmosphere.

traps.Janus: A real Saturn moon, but only about 180 km across, under the 200 km cut-off.
traps.Pan: A Saturn moon only about 30 km across, far below the cut-off.

title: Talons out
q: Daytime birds of prey that breed regularly in the UK
rule: Daytime raptors only (owls don't count), breeding regularly in the UK; winter visitors and rare vagrants don't count.
fact: Red kites were reduced to a small population in mid-Wales by the early 1900s, and they now breed widely across England and Scotland.

traps.Barn owl: A bird of prey, but an owl, and the rule covers daytime birds of prey only.
traps.Rough-legged buzzard: A winter visitor to the UK, not a regular breeder.

title: Hormone hub
q: Endocrine glands that release hormones straight into the blood
rule: Ductless glands only; the organ that also digests food counts for its hormone-making cell clusters, and the reproductive glands count.
fact: The pineal gland is named for its pine-cone shape and makes melatonin, a hormone that helps regulate sleep.

traps.Salivary gland: It's an exocrine gland: it sends saliva out through ducts into the mouth.
traps.Sweat gland: It's an exocrine gland: it releases sweat through ducts onto the skin.

title: Hold that key
q: Keyboard modifier keys that change what other keys do when held
rule: Only keys that act as modifiers when held down; Caps Lock is a toggle and doesn't count.
fact: The Shift key got its name from typewriters, where pressing it shifted the carriage to type capital letters.

traps.Caps Lock: It's a toggle that stays on until pressed again, not a key you hold to change others.
traps.Escape: It's an ordinary key, with no modifier role.

title: Little worlds' company
q: Officially named moons of the dwarf planets Pluto, Eris and Haumea
rule: Only the named moons of Pluto, Eris and Haumea count.
fact: Pluto and its moon Charon are so large relative to each other that they orbit a point in empty space, outside both bodies.

traps.Triton: A big moon, but it orbits Neptune, not a dwarf planet.
traps.Phobos: A moon of Mars, not of any dwarf planet.

title: Cyclone ladder
q: Stages on the US National Hurricane Center's tropical cyclone scale
rule: Give the full stage name, including its number; only the seven stages of the US scale count.
fact: The top category needs sustained winds of at least 157 mph, and only a small number of Atlantic hurricanes have ever reached it.

traps.Category 6: There's no Category 6: winds of 157 mph or more are already Category 5.
traps.Storm: That's a Beaufort force name from the UK Met Office, not a US tropical cyclone stage.

title: Heavy going
q: Imperial units of weight from the avoirdupois system
rule: Avoirdupois units only; the US unit of 2,000 lb is excluded.
fact: A UK hundredweight is 112 pounds, not 100, and a quarter is 28 pounds, which is a quarter of that hundredweight.

traps.Kilogram: It's a metric unit, not part of the imperial system.
traps.Short ton: A US unit of 2,000 lb, not the imperial ton used in the UK.

title: Red planet landers
q: NASA missions that landed on Mars and worked on the surface
rule: Count NASA spacecraft that landed and worked on Mars; a rover carried by another lander, and crashed landers, don't count.
fact: Viking 1 kept sending data from Mars until 1982, about six years after it landed in 1976.

traps.Mars Polar Lander: A NASA lander that crashed in 1999, so it never worked on the surface.
traps.Beagle 2: A British-built lander that was lost after landing in 2003, and it wasn't a NASA mission.
traps.Sojourner: A rover carried by another lander, so the mission name is the answer instead.

title: Uranian heavyweights
q: Moons of Uranus with a diameter over 100 km
rule: Mean diameter must be above 100 km; smaller Uranian moons such as Juliet don't count.
fact: Uranus's moons are named after characters from Shakespeare and Alexander Pope, not from Greek myths.

traps.Juliet: A real Uranus moon, but only about 95 km across, under the 100 km cut-off.
traps.Triton: A large moon, but it orbits Neptune, not Uranus.

title: Scaly and slimy
q: Reptiles and amphibians that are native to the UK
rule: Native species only, including one reintroduced after dying out; introduced foreign species don't count.
fact: The adder is Britain's only venomous snake, though its bite is rarely fatal.

traps.Marsh frog: It was introduced to Britain, so it isn't a native species.
traps.Red-eared slider: A non-native terrapin, not a native British reptile.

title: Long and low
q: Members of the mustelid family living wild in Britain
rule: Counts wild populations of this family, including non-native ones that have escaped or been introduced.
fact: The American mink escaped from fur farms and now preys on water voles across Britain, which has hit the voles hard.

traps.Hedgehog: A spiny insect-eater, not a member of the weasel family.
traps.Fox: A member of the dog family, not the weasel family.

title: Skull session
q: Bones of the adult human skull, excluding the ear bones
rule: Each named bone counts once, whether it comes in a left and right pair or not; the ear ossicles and the hyoid don't count.
fact: The inferior nasal concha is a scroll-shaped bone inside the nose that helps warm and moisten the air you breathe in.

traps.Hyoid: A U-shaped bone in the neck, not part of the skull.
traps.Stapes: A tiny bone of the middle ear, excluded from this set.

title: Sixteen winds
q: The 16 named points of the compass, used for wind direction
rule: The sixteen main points only; the 32-point intermediate names don't count.
fact: Hitchcock's 1959 film North by Northwest takes its title from a compass direction.

traps.North by west: A 32-point compass name, which this set doesn't use.
traps.Northwest by north: A 32-point compass name, not one of the sixteen main points.
